synopsis: The CMS retains existing proximity warnings and automatically brakes if the operator does not act; the intervention ladder spans warning, advice, slowing, stopping and motion inhibition from standstill [f12, f150, f5923]. South African mining regulations require slowing diesel-powered trackless mobile machines to a safe speed before automatic braking when no action is taken, while MOSH specifies warning 2.5–3.0 seconds before intervention and slowing below 10 km/h [f1361, f2441, f2608, f5562]. Mine leaders preferred slowing to a crawl before setting the brake rather than abrupt stops, but warnings only buy response time if operators believe them and the interface enables a response [f3393, f11795, f11843]. Validation should set separate tolerances, thresholds, tests and evidence for each intervention stage, with human simulation examining operator responses to warning, waiting and braking [f2634, f11733, f571]. No universal off-road maximum deceleration, tuning data for standardized automatic slowing interfaces, or evidence for off-road partial service braking was found; escalation should therefore consider remaining stopping margin and uncertainty, including conditions that affect risk, rather than distance alone [f11719, f6508, f6514, f11725]. On-road precedents include a minimum 0.8-second warning and brief haptic brake cues above 4 m/s², but the reviewed off-road legal texts did not establish a 2.0-second warning requirement [f2519, f6498, f2472].
